data.title: AI risks, Reserve Bank of India nudge spur a cybersecurity talent rush
data.description:
Regulated financial entities, including payment aggregators, are likely to step up hiring of chief information security officers (CISOs) as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sharpens its scrutiny of cybersecurity preparedness amid rising attacks and growing threats from artificial intelligence (AI). 
The central bank has been asking entities during routine audits whether they have a CISO, while the shortage of experienced cybersecurity professionals threatens to leave smaller players particularly exposed, industry executives said. 
The growing demand for specialised expertise is also reflected in recruitment at State Bank of India (SBI), the country’s largest lender, which has invited applications for six senior positions spanning artificial intelligence (AI), analytics, governance and architecture, with annual compensation of up to ₹1.6 crore. The hiring underscores the premium financial institutions are placing on specialised technology and risk-management capabilities as cyber threats become more sophisticated. 
“During routine audits, the RBI is now checking if the company has a CISO so that it has a point of contact to resolve any concerns. The regulator is also checking with companies whether we can innovate on AI itself as a defence against AI-led offences that we have seen in the past few weeks,” said a senior executive at a payment aggregator. 
A CISO is a senior executive responsible for an organisation’s information and cybersecurity. In financial institutions, the role spans protecting systems, networks and customer data, ensuring regulatory compliance, managing cyber risks and overseeing incident response.  
“More CISO involvement is certainly required. The CSITE (the RBI’s Cyber Security and Information Technology Examination Cell) surveys and inspections conducted by the RBI are already focused on CISOs,” said a senior banker at a large private sector bank. 
But the industry faces a significant talent constraint. The banking and non-banking financial company (NBFC) sector comprises hundreds of players, and India lacks the depth of CISO talent needed to address the vulnerabilities emerging across the system, the banker said. 
While larger institutions may be better placed to attract experienced professionals, smaller entities could struggle to compete. “First, the required talent has to be available. Second, that talent must be willing to work with smaller players. There also needs to be continuous capability building and investment in technology,” the banker said. 
An email sent to the RBI seeking comment did not elicit a response till press time. 
SBI’s recruitment drive covers one post each of general manager and chief AI officer; deputy general manager (DGM) in risk and operational analytics; DGM in AI governance and compliance; DGM in data engineering; model application development and AI ops; AI solution architect; and enterprise AI architect. The general manager and chief AI officer position carries an annual cost to company (CTC) of up to ₹1.6 crore, while the three DGM positions offer up to ₹1.2 crore each. The two architect positions carry annual CTC of up to ₹90 lakh each. 
The RBI has also recently asked banks, small finance banks (SFBs) and NBFCs to strengthen controls around application programming interfaces (APIs), tighten safeguards for third-party systems and improve monitoring of fund transfers as cyberattacks targeting financial institutions increase. 
A key concern is the exploitation of vulnerabilities in third-party systems connected to banks and NBFCs. In some cases, fraudsters have compromised financial entities’ systems to divert money through banking channels. In others, beneficiary account details in loan disbursement systems have been manipulated, resulting in funds being transferred to accounts controlled by fraudsters. 
The shortage of cybersecurity expertise is not confined to India. According to Fortinet’s 2026 Cybersecurity Skills Gap report, based on a survey of 2,750 IT and cybersecurity decision-makers across 32 locations, including India, 51 per cent of organisations said senior-level cybersecurity skills were their biggest requirement. 
In the Asia-Pacific region, 66 per cent of respondents said finding candidates with AI experience in cybersecurity was a challenge. A lack of cybersecurity skills and trained staff was the most frequently cited cause of breaches, at 56 per cent. Only half of respondents said their board members were fully aware of AI-related risks. 
The shortage could have implications beyond individual institutions, given the financial system’s growing interconnectedness and reliance on technology service providers and other third-party vendors. “Given that the financial ecosystem is interconnected, with institutions being counterparties to one another in different ways, the weakest link in the chain can pose a risk to multiple players in the system,” a source cautioned.

data.title: Over 80% Indian firms yet to see AI gains: PwC chief Sanjeev Krishan
data.description:
There is a substantial opportunity for reaping gains from artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-enabled tools, since more than 80 per cent of enterprises have yet to see any real gains from its implementation, said Sanjeev Krishan, chairperson, PwC India.  
 
For the remaining 20 per cent that saw some productivity gains from applying AI, the total addressable market has barely been touched, Krishan told Business Standard in an exclusive interaction after the launch of PwC India’s Future AI Experience Lab in Gurugram.
 
“It is not just a question of efficiency. For companies, it is also a question of whether investments in and for AI will succeed in their environment as well,” Krishan said, adding just copying investments may lead to some productivity gains in the short run but can expose enterprises to other issues.
 
He also spoke about the need for companies, particularly conglomerates, to prepare for compliance with various provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, which has a May 2027 implementation deadline, by developing and implementing bespoke solutions to comply with the various provisions.
 
“Because they are conglomerates, they have multiple touchpoints and multiple places where they have stored their data. For them, it is about having solutions for each of these silos,” Krishan said.
 
Most companies in India and across the globe are no longer thinking about AI solely in terms of the return on investments, but have also expanded their approach to include security and safety of data as a primary concern over the last few months, he said. 
 
Despite the pace of technological developments in AI, the diffusion of this technology for the greater good of humanity will still take time as enterprises grapple with challenges such as cost, change management, and the actual gains from AI, Krishan said.
 
“I am not talking about the diffusion of AI to make my emailing more productive. Four out of five companies have not really embraced AI in a way that leads to some productivity gains,” he said.
 
In addition to working out the complex challenges of cost, change management, and figuring out the actual gains from AI, enterprises today also lack the “full conviction” that the technology can be applied at scale to solve their issues, Krishan said.
 
The creation of the Future AI Experiences Lab is one step toward solving that problem for enterprises by showing them real-world implementations of the problems they face and working on them in a “co-creation” mode, he said, adding that these would also be ope­ned in Bengaluru and Mumbai. “My intention with this Lab is that I should be able to host at least two clients per week and work with them on whatever value and efficiency they are trying to create in a safe micro-environment by using synthetic data provided by them. The clients could be big or small firms, startups, disruptors, anyone,” he said.
 
The lab houses 90 industry and sector-specific AI assets and also brings PwC's India expertise and alliance ecosystem to demonstrate the practical applications.

data.title: Bank-based brokers lead India's margin trading facility market, shows data
data.description:
Traditional and bank-backed brokerage firms continue to dominate India’s margin trading facility (MTF) market, commanding a significantly larger share than new-age discount brokers.
 
Bank-backed players like ICICI Securities and Kotak Securities account for 17 per cent and 15 per cent of the MTF market, respectively. 
 
HDFC Securities holds a 9 per cent share, bringing the combined share of these three pla­yers to 41 per cent as of Oct­ober. In comparison, Zerodha and Groww command shares of 6 and 3 per cent, respectively, according to a Jefferies report. Even traditional firms such as Motilal Oswal and Axis Direct have a combined MTF share of 10 per cent, according to the report.  
 
 
The growing traction in MTF comes as investors increasingly use leverage to build cash equity positions, with brokers funding a part of the purchase value in return for interest income. Interest rates can vary across brokers from 6 per cent per annum to as much as 20 per cent. 
 
After derivatives fuelled the growth of a new generation of discount brokers, MTF is emerging as another potential revenue driver for the broking industry, where the majority share has returned to traditional players. NSE’s MTF book has risen to ~1.47 trillion as of Thursday. It stood at a record of 1.51 trillion as of September end this year, rapidly growing compared to ~99,446 crore by end-September 2025.

data.title: India Inc responds to PM Modi's call, seeks greater regulatory transparency
data.description:
Days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticised Indian industry for falling short on job creation and other fronts, senior officials of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) on Monday outlined steps the government could take to boost private investment, including strengthening market integrity, improving regulatory transparency and easing the flow of cross-border capital. 
“The key strategy of the government must be to create a business environment characterised by robust investor protection and regulatory ease coupled by market integrity. Towards this objective, regulatory authorities would play a key role by ensuring that their compliances do not stand as an obstacle for the free flow of cross border capital,” said CII Director General Chandrajit Banerjee, in a post on X. 
 
He said Modi’s call for industry to invest more, foster innovation and improve competitiveness was a strong reminder of the need to raise productivity and secure long-term economic growth. “India’s ability to attract long-term capital will be determined by the strength of its markets and the competitiveness of our industries. Increased transparency, along with ease of doing business, will strengthen India’s standing as a global investment destination,” he added. 
Addressing the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry’s (Ficci’s) annual general meeting last week, Modi criticised Indian companies for their continued reliance on imports in critical sectors and for treating the country’s vast domestic market as a “comfort zone”, rather than improving product quality and building capabilities to compete globally. 
Rajiv Memani, CII’s immediate past president, said global investors sought clear, predictable and proportionate rules. “India’s regulatory framework must deliver on all three. India will need both domestic savings and foreign capital to finance its investment requirements. Long-term global investors weigh regulatory clarity, predictability and compliance costs alongside returns,” he said. 
He further said openness to global capital and market integrity are complementary objectives.  
Sanjiv Puri, former CII president and chairman and managing director of ITC, said strong corporate governance and predictable regulation were essential for Indian companies seeking to attract long-term domestic and foreign capital. “Transparency, investor confidence and ease of investment” reinforced one another, he said, adding that “vibrant markets can give a significant impetus to robust economic growth and competitiveness”. 
R Dinesh, another former CII president and executive chairman of TVS Supply Chain Solutions, said access to long-term capital and confidence in market regulation were crucial for an economy investing heavily in infrastructure and logistics. “Clear rules, strong governance and proportionate regulation can help deliver both,” he suggested. 
CII President R Mukundan, who is also managing director and chief executive officer of Tata Chemicals, said the next priority was to move beyond ease of doing business to the “speed of doing business”. CII’s Private Investment Barometer showed that private project announcements reached a record ₹26.6 trillion in the first half of FY27, 4.4 times the long-run average, he said.
As the prime minster Modi has said, “the task now is for industry to make ‘India First’ the basis of every long-term decision. CIl and its members are committed to this agenda,” he added.

data.title: Uber pilots Connected Journeys in Delhi, eyes pan-India rollout in 2027
data.description:
Ride-hailing platform Uber is piloting its ‘Connected Journeys’ feature in Delhi, allowing commuters to combine metro travel with first- and last-mile options such as three-wheelers and two-wheelers through a single journey plan on its app. The company plans to expand the feature across India by early next year.
 
The feature brings different modes of transport together, enabling riders to view route options, estimated travel times and fares across various legs of their journey and book the relevant services within the Uber app.
 
Using customer and trip data, the platform will also suggest whether a bike, auto-rickshaw or cab would be a suitable option for the first or last mile, depending on the journey. However, riders will have the flexibility to manually switch between the available modes.
 
 
The pilot is currently underway in Delhi, with a wider rollout planned in phases. Uber already enables metro ticket bookings through its app in several cities.
 
Connected Journeys is part of Uber’s broader push towards integrated, multimodal mobility, as urban commuters increasingly look to combine public transport with app-based services to navigate congested cities.
 
Commenting on the initiative, Aditya Kapoor, director of supply operations at Uber India & South Asia, said, “Connected Journeys is one way we can help bring those modes together, making it easier for riders to combine Metro with Uber for the first and last mile and complete their journeys more seamlessly.”

data.title: For gig and platform workers, welfare promises remain a distant reality
data.description:
Rani, a 25-year-old Delhi-based gig worker for an on-demand home services platform, works almost every day. Between bookings, it’s a struggle to find rest areas or washrooms. 
This year, Rani developed kidney stones — the result, doctors say, of working long hours without washroom facilities. Her treatment cost her ₹20,000, a significant expense for her. 
“The company talks about providing insurance, but the terms and conditions make it very difficult for me to claim it. Eligibility is also linked to our performance metrics. The apps offer little assistance in helping me understand the process or navigate the technical requirements,” she said. 
A September 2026 nationwide survey of 1,000 platform workers across 10 cities by labour rights organisations Janpahal and the Gig Workers Association (GigWA) found that extreme weather, road accidents and long working hours were major concerns. Of the 778 workers who reported working in extreme weather, 96.6 per cent said heat affected their ability to work. 
They reported health problems such as dehydration, exhaustion and severe overheating. Among workers reporting safety incidents, 62.2 per cent had experienced near-misses with vehicles, 38 per cent had injuries due to road conditions and 27.5 per cent were involved in traffic accidents. 
The survey also found that 62.2 per cent of workers did not have health insurance and 44.2 per cent lacked accident insurance. More than 80 per cent of those who tried to claim accident insurance found the process difficult. 
Only a framework 
In the absence of an operational central social security scheme for gig and platform workers, insurance coverage remains largely dependent on individual platforms and the terms and eligibility conditions of their policies. While the Code on Social Security, 2020, provides a framework for extending benefits such as health and accident insurance, the specific scheme to operationalise these benefits is yet to be notified. 
In October, nearly a year after the new labour laws became operational, the Centre notified the National Social Security Board for gig and platform workers. The board is to recommend welfare schemes, advise the Centre on administering the Code, monitor social security schemes and review state-level record-keeping mechanisms and expenditure from the Social Security Fund, the proposed fund for financing social security benefits for gig platform and informal workers. 
The Code provides for life, disability and accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, and old-age protection. It allows aggregators — those employing gig workers — to contribute 1-2 per cent of their annual revenue to the Social Security Fund, capped at 5 per cent of the amount paid or payable to workers. 
However, the rate and commencement date are yet to be notified. 
A key challenge will be determining workers’ eligibility and calculating their benefits. Under the notified rules, workers must have been engaged with a single aggregator for at least 90 days in a financial year, or for 120 days across multiple aggregators.
For workers with irregular or seasonal engagement, these thresholds could mean losing access to benefits even when platform work is their primary source of income. Nitesh Kumar Das, organising secretary of GigWA, said workers who suffered an accident before completing the prescribed engagement threshold could be left without protection. 
“Basic health and accident insurance should begin from the date of registration, with additional benefits expanding as workers accumulate engagement credits rather than depending on a single eligibility cut-off,” Das said. 
Shaik Salauddin, cofounder and national general secretary of the Indian Federation of App-Based Transport Workers (IFAT), which is represented on the board, said the proposed schemes should cover health, accident and life insurance, pensions and family welfare. 
“Social security benefits should be available to all gig and platform workers without exclusions based on below-poverty-line status, income limits or income tax return filings. The benefits recommended for gig workers should also not be lower than those already provided by individual platforms,” Salauddin said. 
How to count gig work? 
The eligibility challenge is compounded by the transactional nature of gig work. Unlike regular employment, where provident fund contributions are calculated monthly against an employee’s salary, gig workers can move between platforms, take up assignments intermittently or combine platform work with formal employment. 
“There is no common shared ledger between platforms. So how do you compute eligibility? If you work for 90 days with a platform, it is still easy to compute the benefits, but if you work for 120 days across multiple platforms, how do you calculate that? The infrastructure is needed to be able to provide social security to gig workers. Their benefits will need to be calculated, corrected, deposited, disbursed and accounted for,” said Rishi Agrawal, cofounder and chief executive officer of TeamLease RegTech. 
Agrawal said workers completing one order a day and those completing 100 could have different earnings and engagement. He questioned whether contributions should be calculated per transaction or through periodic reporting, saying the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation’s batch-based compliance model might not suit gig work. 
A common digital identity and reporting system could help address fragmented records. Kuljeet Singh, chief financial officer of GI Group Holding, said Aadhaar-linked registration and the Universal Account Number (UAN) could provide a basis for portability, but platforms and staffing companies would need to report workers’ engagement and payouts through a common system. 
Follow the worker 
“Contributions should follow the worker, not the job. A delivery partner could work on two apps and then take up a three-month warehouse assignment through a staffing firm. Their records would be split across different systems. There needs to be a common reporting standard for engagement days and payouts, with platforms and staffing companies sharing this information electronically, preferably through APIs rather than periodic uploads,” Singh said. 
He said the system would also need a common definition of an engagement day, based on whether a worker logs into an application, completes a task or earns a minimum amount. Benefits should reflect actual earnings, with credits accumulating at each payout and eligibility assessed annually. Accident and life cover could begin once a worker is registered and active, while other benefits build with sustained engagement. 
For workers, access to these records would be as important as the system used to calculate contributions. Das called for the government’s e-Shram portal to consolidate work histories and earnings across platforms and allow workers to correct inaccurate records. 
The portal had just over 1 million registered gig and platform workers as of July 19, 2026, according to a parliamentary reply. Meanwhile, NITI Aayog had projected the gig workforce to reach 12.7 million in 2024-25 and 14.3 million
in 2025-26. 
Agrawal said workers also lacked a common passbook-like facility to track contributions and entitlements, unlike Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) subscribers. “Trust as a currency has not been established yet with gig workers’ social security. There is no passbook system and this kind of transparency will have to be established,” he said. 
Another concern is whether aggregators could pass on the cost of their social security contributions through lower incentives, bonuses or per-order payments, reducing workers’ take-home earnings. Das called for independent monitoring to ensure workers did not bear the cost of contributions mandated for aggregators. 
The coexistence of central and state-level welfare frameworks could add to compliance challenges. Rajasthan, Karnataka, Telangana, Bihar and Jharkhand have introduced their own laws for gig workers, with different approaches to welfare funds, aggregator contributions and worker protections. 
 
Telangana launched its gig-worker welfare policy and an online registration facility on November 14, providing for a unique identity across platforms and accident-related compensation of up to ₹10 lakh. 
Agrawal said platforms would need to undertake state-level revenue reconciliation to determine where contributions were due, with central and state systems operating alongside each other without overlapping compliance requirements. 
Other challenges 
Responsibility for contributions could become more complicated when workers move between platform-based assignments and formal employment. A worker may be engaged by a staffing firm, deployed through a contractor and work at a client’s establishment. 
“In staffing, the difficulty is the number of layers. A worker may be sourced by one firm, deployed through a sub-contractor, and work at a client’s warehouse or on its app. Each party can easily assume someone else is paying,” Singh said. 
He called for a clear liability matrix specifying the responsibility of different entities and revised staffing contracts to account for additional compliance costs and prevent contributions from being missed or counted twice. 
The National Social Security Board provides an institutional mechanism to take these issues forward, experts say. Its effectiveness will depend on whether a common system can identify workers, reconcile contributions and ensure benefits remain accessible as they move between platforms, jobs and states.

data.title: ₹30,707 cr mcap erased as deal rattles Tata Steel, APL Apollo shareholders
data.description:
The proposed Tata Steel-APL Apollo Tubes transaction has triggered an unusual market reaction, with shares of both the acquirer and the target falling sharply after the deal announcement. Tata Steel plunged nearly 8.2 per cent on Monday, making it the biggest percentage loser among Sensex and Nifty 50 constituents. APL Apollo Tubes, meanwhile, was the worst-performing midcap stock, shedding 21.4 per cent of its market capitalisation. 
Together, the two companies lost ₹30,707 crore in market value. 
In large corporate transactions, typically either the acquirer’s shares fall because investors consider the purchase price excessive, or the seller’s stock declines because the offer undervalues its business. In this case, both came under pressure, with analysts pointing to the deal’s complex structure and the substantial additional debt it will saddle the companies with. 
Under the transaction, APL Apollo will first acquire Tata Steel’s tubes and colour-coated businesses for ₹28,000 crore, funded through borrowings. In the second leg, Tata Steel will acquire majority control of the enlarged APL Apollo Tubes for around ₹32,267 crore by purchasing shares from the promoters and making an open offer to minority shareholders. 
The first leg is likely to add about ₹28,000 crore to APL Apollo’s debt, while Tata Steel’s liabilities are expected to rise by around ₹4,200 crore. If APL Apollo becomes a subsidiary following the transaction, its borrowings will also be reflected in Tata Steel’s consolidated debt. Tata Steel reported consolidated gross debt of ₹1.02 trillion at the end of September. 
 
 
 
The financing burden could be particularly onerous for APL Apollo. Bankers estimate that the company will have to pay ₹2,800-3,900 crore annually in interest on the ₹28,000 crore acquisition loan, assuming borrowing costs of 10-14 per cent. This compares with operating profit, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda), of ₹1,914 crore reported by APL Apollo in FY26, leaving little financial headroom to service the debt while maintaining profitability. 
Analysts say the clearest beneficiaries of the transaction are APL Apollo’s existing promoters, the Sanjay Gupta family, who stand to receive around ₹15,510 crore for their 26.6 per cent stake. In addition, SG Tech Engineering, a company owned by APL Apollo's promoters, will set up exclusive contract manufacturing facilities with a capacity of 5 million tonnes for colour-coated products to supply Tata Steel. 
The deal offers limited apparent benefits to shareholders of either company, said Shriram Subramanian, founder and managing director of InGovern Research Services. “The transaction doesn’t seem beneficial to either Tata Steel shareholders or APL Apollo minority shareholders. Tata Steel is paying a huge premium to acquire APL Apollo’s business, while the latter will be borrowing nearly ₹28,000 crore to acquire Tata Steel’s colour-coated and steel tube business as part of the transaction,” he said. 
Subramanian said the APL Apollo promoters stood to gain from both the sale proceeds and the opportunity to establish a substantial contract manufacturing business supplying colour-coated products to Tata Steel. 
Amit Tandon, founder and managing director of Institutional Investor Advisory Services India, questioned the strategic rationale for Tata Steel. “If Tata Steel intends to become an integrated steel manufacturer, why would it choose to depend on a contract manufacturer for a significant portion of its colour-coated products? And it achieves this dependency after adding around ₹32,000 crore to its consolidated debt,” he said. 
Tandon also questioned the transaction’s approval mechanism, saying minority shareholders of neither company would get an opportunity to vote on the deal. “My reading of the provisions of the Companies Act suggests that institutional shareholders will not get the opportunity to express their opinion on this transaction, which is not a good thing,” he said.

data.title: For tariff classification, section and chapter titles have no legal force
data.description:
I refer to your article ‘Scotch at the Docks’, which appeared on November 16, where you have mentioned about the classification 21069051 for compound alcoholic preparations. I don’t understand why that item is under Chapter 21, which is for ‘miscellaneous edible preparations’, whereas there is a separate chapter 22 specifically for ‘beverages, spirits and vinegar’. Please clarify.
 
Rule 1 of the General Rules for Interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 says that “the titles of sections, chapters and sub-chapters are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes”. So, for classification, please do not go by the chapter or section titles only. Please go by the wording of the headings, subheadings and tariff items read with the relevant section and chapter notes and where necessary, the Interpretative Notes.  
Secondly, please note that the tariff item 21069051 expressly covers qualifying ‘compound alcoholic preparations of a kind used to manufacture beverages’ and not the beverages. The distinction is between a preparation used to make a beverage and a beverage classifiable under Chapter 22. 
I refer to your article ‘New FEMA rules bring small service exporters into the reporting net’ which appeared on November 4, wherein you have said that “even small service providers like individuals engaged in online teaching of music and yoga are required to furnish form EDF to the bank”. Our bankers say that it is not necessary to do so. Can you please clarify. 
The position stated in my October 4, 2026 article was correct under the regulations as they stood on that date. The Reserve Bank of India subsequently amended Regulation 3(2) by a notification dated November 2, 2026, effective from October 1, 2026. Under the amended rule, a resident individual exporting services is deemed to have furnished the EDF upon giving the authorised dealer the information it requires to credit the inward re­mittance.  
Your bankers are therefore right under the amended regulations. A separate EDF is unnecessary. 
We had exported certain goods by claiming duty drawback and RoDTEP duty credits. Soon after exporting, we found that we had packed the goods wrongly and so, recalled the consignment for repacking and re-export. Now, we cannot use the notification 158/95-Cus dated November 14, 1995, because that is for repairs, reconditioning, reprocessing. Use of S. No.1 of notification no. 45/2017-Cus dated  June 30, 2017 would involve surrender of the export benefits and after Customs clearance and repacking, sending the goods as a fresh export claiming the benefits afresh. Is there a better way? 
Yes. A warehousing route is available. File an into-bond bill of entry and move the goods to a bonded warehouse where you can ask for permission to repack the goods  for exports. After repacking, you can re-export the goods under Section 69 without payment of import duty, subject to its conditions, by filing an ex-bond shipping bill. In this route, you need not surrender any export benefits availed.

smechat@bsmail.in

data.title: Bernstein upgrades Nvidia stock to outperform as Jensen Huang returns
data.description:
Analysts at Bernstein led by Stacy A. Rasgon, Arpad von Nemes and Alrick Shaw upgraded Nvidia stock to ‘outperform’ after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief-executive, effective immediately. The counter surged over 30 per cent in pre-market trade. Tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 7 per cent.
 
Meanwhile, Bernstein had downgraded Nvidia's stock to Market Perform 11 days ago when it looked likely that Huang's conduct would see his removal from the company.
 
"As we remain positive on AI buildout fundamentals, and with Jensen back in the seat, we upgrade today back to outperform (as his exit was the primary reason for the downgrade)," analysts at Bernstein wrote in the report. 
ALSO READ: Nvidia stock skyrockets 29% as board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
 
 
Adding: "Nevertheless, current valuation, with Jensen at the helm, seem supportive enough to us for now. We are going to leave our price target at $200 (~10x our CY28/29 average EPS), which seems to reflect a decent amount of potential downside. We upgrade to Outperform," the Bernstein note said.
 
News of Huang's removal had wiped more than $1 trillion off Nvidia this month, with the shares plunging as much as 14 per cent in a single session, even as the chipmaker posted record quarterly sales of $115.8 billion, double a year earlier, and profits that also doubled to $65.3 billion.
 
Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group - a global consulting firm that has nearly $12 billion worth of assets under management, too, believes that the reinstatement sends out a strong signal to the stock markets, and suggests that the stock can double in value from the current levels going ahead. 
ALSO READ: Nvidia board made right call on Jensen Huang reinstatement, says Trump
 
"I believe Nvidia could double from here. Washington wanted Huang back, this move has the White House’s fingerprints all over it, and it got him back. The White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry. His return hands him more control than ever. He’s got the backing of the board, the US President and the market, and that’s a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level,” Green said. 
 
While Huang, according to reports, still faces closed-door questioning from three House committees on 1 December over Nvidia’s chips and export controls, Green believes the backing he now has from Washington puts him in a commanding position.

data.title: Razorpay payout disruption puts spotlight on payment security
data.description:
Payouts on fintech major Razorpay’s business banking platform, RazorpayX, faced disrup­tion last week with the company telling its merchants that upgrades at its banking partner were “taking longer than expected”, according to three sources and an email reviewed by Business Standard.
 
In the notice dated November 18, Razorpay said payout services would resume “within the next 7 days” and that merchants’ funds were “safe and fully accounted for”.   
“We, together with our banking partner, are implementing technical upgrades to payouts, resulting in the ongo­ing downtime. Re-enabling your payouts remains our highest priority and our teams are working around the clock, including weekends, to restore payout services for you. But the upgrades are taking longer than expected,” the email said. 
Razorpay did not respond to detailed queries emailed by Business Standard. Emails sent to Axis Bank, IDFC First Bank, RBL Bank, and Yes Bank did not elicit a response. 
Payouts are the money a business sends out, usua­lly sent in bulk and automatically, via a payments firm’s platform linked to their bank account. 
Banks and payment firms have tightened checks on payout systems across the industry in recent weeks, an industry executive said, slowing some transfers. When  attackers gain access to a firm’s payout systems, they can send money out of its accounts from its own compromised servers, avoiding detection.
